behave is a Python tool that runs tests written as plain-text examples. In your project, each example shows one
requirement or one constraint (RF ID) of your system with data and a known answer. This page takes you from a
first draft to tests that run against your system on AWS. You need only the level that your checkpoint asks for.

| Level | When you need it | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| [Level 0](#level-0) | Checkpoint 1 | Write draft rules and examples, and check them with a dry run. You do not write code. |
| [Level 1](#level-1) | Checkpoint 2 (proposed) | Write the Python function behind each step, and run the examples. |
| [Level 2](#level-2) | Later (proposed) | Use ready steps from the course kit for the simulator, DuckDB queries and evals: runs of the answers of an LLM (large language model; we also say *the model*) on cases with known answers. |
| [Level 3](#level-3) | Later (proposed) | Run chosen examples on AWS, and make an eval a gate: an example that fails when fewer runs are correct than the number you chose. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,22,64]"}

Levels 1 to 3 are proposed and may change before Checkpoint 2.

The examples on this page come from the rides example of the [Checkpoint 1](project-checkpoint1.qmd) page: a
ride-hailing app in New York whose trip events (a trip is requested, accepted, completed) reach the system of a
team t00. The whole example is the repository [cp1-example](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/cp1-example/tree/cp1), tag
`cp1`. Run the Level 0, Level 2 and Level 3 commands in a terminal at the root of your repository. The Level 1
example has a folder of its own, and its steps say where to work. The outputs on this page come from behave 1.3.3,
and every command pins that version (`uvx behave@1.3.3`) because older versions do not read `Rule:`: behave 1.2.6
stops with a `ParserError` at the first `Rule:` line.

## Level 0 (Checkpoint 1): draft rules and examples without code {#level-0}

At this level you write files in **Gherkin**, the plain-text format that behave reads, and check that behave can
read them, before any Python code exists. Each file is a **feature file**: its name ends in `.feature`, and it
holds one `Feature:`. In it:

- a **rule** (`Rule:`) states one requirement, and carries its ID as a tag;
- an **example** (`Example:`) under a rule shows the rule with data and an answer that you know before the system
  runs. `Example:` is another word for `Scenario:`, and behave's output says "scenario";
- an example is written as **steps**: lines that start with `Given`, `When`, `Then`, `And` or `But`. The `Given`
  sets up the data and the state before, the `When` is the event or the question, and the `Then` is what must be
  true after ([behave: Given, When, Then](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#given-when-then-and-but)).

`Examples:` with an s is a different thing: the table of a `Scenario Outline`.

### Folder layout

behave looks for a folder named `features/` at the root of your repository, and inside it for a folder named
`steps/` ([behave: feature testing layout](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#feature-testing-layout)).
The `steps/` folder holds Python files at Level 1. At Level 0 it holds one empty file, so that git keeps the folder.

1. Create both folders and the empty file:

   ```default
   mkdir -p features/steps
   touch features/steps/.gitkeep
   ```

2. Check the result with `ls -a features features/steps`. You should see `steps` in the first list and `.gitkeep`
   in the second.

When your feature files are written, the layout of the rides example is:

```default
features/
├── js01_trips_per_zone.feature     serves JS01
├── js01_yesterdays_trips.feature   serves JS01
├── js04_pickup_place.feature       serves JS04, with the assistant
├── trip_assignment.feature         serves JS02 and JS03
└── steps/
    ├── .gitkeep                    empty at Level 0
    └── pickup_steps.py             in the example only (see the dry run below)
```

### Job stories and feature files

A job story can need more than one feature file, and one feature file can serve more than one job story:

- **By default, write one feature file for each job story you plan to implement**, named for what the user gets, and tag
  its `Feature:` with the story's ID (`@JS01`).
- **Split a story into two feature files** when the user gets two different things from it. Each feature's description
  says which part of the story it covers. In the example, the analyst of JS01 gets the trips requested in each
  zone and, each morning, yesterday's completed trips: two feature files.
- **Share a feature file between two stories** when both users read the same thing. It carries both tags
  (`@JS02 @JS03`), and a requirement that both stories share has its rule once, in that feature file. In the example,
  the driver (JS02) and the rider (JS03) read the same assignment of a trip to a driver.
- **A story tag on a feature says that every rule in it serves that story.** When one rule serves one more story,
  put that story's tag on the rule.

A feature file named "Constraints", or after an ID, does not name anything a user gets. Put the rule of each RF in
the feature file of the job story that the constraint is about.

### One rule for each ID

Each R ID in `docs/requirements.md`, and each RF ID whose line ends with a `[Scenario](…)` link, gets one
`Rule:` in one feature file, tagged with its ID:
`@R020` for your own requirement R020, `@RF010` for the constraint RF010 of your proposal feedback issue. Under the
rule goes at least one `Example:`. RQ IDs, and RF IDs whose line ends with `Read:` or `Read at Checkpoint 2:`, do not get a rule.

1. Create `features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature`, or use a file name that fits your story. You should see the file
   in `features/`.
2. Put the story's tag, `Feature:` with a name, and a sentence on what part of the story the feature covers. behave
   does not run this text: it is there for the person who reads the file.
3. Add one rule with its ID as a tag, and one example under it, as shown below, and save the file. Indent the lines
   as shown, with spaces. The table's columns are fields of a trip request: `event_id` is one ID for one event,
   `trip_id` is one ID for one trip, `pickup_zone_id` is the zone the rider is in, `event_time` is when the rider
   asked, and `received_time` is when the event reached the system.

The file below is a shortened version of the example's `features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature`: two lines of its
description, and one of the three examples of [its rule for R020](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/cp1-example/blob/cp1/features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature?plain=1#L22-L45).

```gherkin
@JS01
Feature: Trips requested in each zone
  Covers the first part of JS01 (operations analyst): the number of trips requested in each pickup zone for each
  5-minute period. A period holds the requests with an event time from its start up to, and not including, its end.

  @R020
  Rule: If a request is received after its period ended, then the system shall add it to the stored count of the period of its event time, and store a count of 1 if its zone does not have a count for that period yet

    Example: Request received 7 minutes late
      Given only these trip requests are received:
        | event_id  | trip_id | pickup_zone_id | event_time           | received_time        |
        | ev-000011 | t-0011  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:01:10Z | 2026-11-23T09:01:11Z |
        | ev-000012 | t-0012  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:04:00Z | 2026-11-23T09:11:00Z |
      When the time is 2026-11-23T09:11:30Z
      Then zone 161 has 2 trips requested between 09:00 and 09:05
```

The rule is the requirement R020 of `docs/requirements.md` in sentence case: it says what the system shall do. The example's answer, 2, follows from its
table: request ev-000012 has an event time of 09:04, inside the period from 09:00 to 09:05, and was received
7 minutes later, at 09:11. The `When` is 30 s after that receipt, inside R020's target of data latency under 60 s at p95 for a
late request; one example checks one such request.

### Tags

`@JS01`, `@R020` and `@RF010` are **tags**: labels that start with `@`, on the line above a feature, a rule or an
example. A tag reaches everything under it: the examples of a rule carry the rule's tag, and every example of a
feature carries the feature's tag. To dry-run only the examples of one ID, name its tag:
`uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run --tags=R020` ([behave: tag expressions](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tag_expressions/)).

When one of your own requirements is how you meet an RF, write one rule with both tags. In the example, R080
(refuse the second accept of a trip) meets RF030 (two drivers accept the same trip at the same moment), so its
rule is tagged `@R080 @RF030`.

`@RF010` above a rule is a tag: a label that `--tags` selects and reports show. `@given` above a Python function
(Level 1) is a decorator: it makes the function a step.

behave gives special meaning to only a few tags: `@wip` when you run `behave --wip`
([behave: works in progress](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/#works-in-progress)), and tags that
start with `@fixture.` or active tags such as `@use.with_`, but only when `features/environment.py` sets them up
([behave: tags in Python](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#accessing-tag-information-in-python),
[behave: active tags](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/new_and_noteworthy_v1.2.5/#active-tags)). ID tags
such as `@R010` and `@RF010` are plain labels, and so are `@eval` and `@live` at this level.

### From an EARS line to a rule and its examples {#ears}

Each R line of `docs/requirements.md` is written in [EARS](https://alistairmavin.com/ears/) form: an optional
opening such as `WHEN <trigger>`, then `THE SYSTEM SHALL` and what the system does. The form says where each part
goes in the example:

| EARS form | In the example |
|---|---|
| `WHEN <trigger> THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>` | the trigger is the `When`, the response is the `Then`, and the `Given` holds the data before |
| `WHILE <state> THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>` | the state is in the `Given` (the data) and the time of the `When`; the response is the `Then`. An example shows one moment of the state |
| `IF <problem> THEN THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>` | the problem is an injected fault in the `Given` (the same `event_id` twice, a late `received_time`); when the problem is the request itself, such as a value out of range, it is the `When` |
| `THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>` | the rule's sentence is the requirement; choose two examples that differ in something that could break it |
| `WHERE <feature> THE SYSTEM SHALL <response>` | a tag on the feature that names the option, such as `@assistant` |
| the target after `\|` (data latency under 60 s at p95) | one case of it in the `Then` ("within 30 s", inside the target), or a time in the `When` chosen so that the answer must already hold; the percentile needs many cases |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,66]"}

Write each `Rule:` line with the EARS form and meaning of its R line, in sentence case, so that it says what the
system shall do (`When a 5-minute period ends, the system shall store one count …`); an RF line becomes
`The system shall …`. Name only the situation in an `Example:` title
and leave the outcome to its `Then`: not `A request at the end of a period is in the next period`, but
`A request exactly at the end of a period (09:05:00)`.

The answer of an example (2 trips) is not a requirement; the target from the R line (data latency under 60 s at p95) is. The times
in an example are data: nobody waits for them.

### Data in an example

An example gets its data from a table inside it or from a simulated data set:

- **A table inside the example**, for a few hand-picked events. Its columns are the fields of the event, as the
  event fields of the `## Data` section of your `docs/design.md` list them, and the first row holds their names. Use it
  when 2 or 3 events show the rule, as in the R020 example above. The word "only" in
  `Given only these trip requests are received` says that the table holds all the requests of the example.
- **A simulated data set**, for the cases where the number of events matters, such as a whole hour or a whole
  file: events or files that your team will generate from a real data set, so that a test knows every event that
  was sent. Name it by its ID and name: `Given the simulated data set SIM01 "rush-hour"`. At Checkpoint 1 the data
  set is a bullet of words in the `## Data` section; its example is read by the dry run like any other.

```gherkin
    Example: One simulated hour with 4 requests delivered twice
      Given the simulated data set SIM01 "rush-hour"
      When the counts are read at 2026-11-23T10:11:00Z
      Then zones 48, 161 and 230 show 304, 191 and 342 trips requested between 09:00 and 10:00
```

Put the data of each example in the example itself, not in a `Background`: a reader then sees the data and the
answer together.

### How to write a good example

#### Describe what the system must do, not what a person clicks

An example stays true when you change a page or rename a button. Write the data in the `Given`, the one event or
question in the `When`, and the result that a user or another system can observe in the `Then`
([behave: Then](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#then)).

This example describes clicks, and its `Then` does not have anything that a test can compare:

```gherkin
    Example: Check the counts
      Given I open the dashboard and click "Refresh"
      When I wait for the page to load
      Then the counts look right
```

This example describes the same requirement as behaviour:

```gherkin
    Example: One request delivered twice
      Given only these trip requests are received:
        | event_id  | trip_id | pickup_zone_id | event_time           | received_time        |
        | ev-000101 | t-0101  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:11:00Z | 2026-11-23T09:11:01Z |
        | ev-000102 | t-0102  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:12:30Z | 2026-11-23T09:12:31Z |
        | ev-000101 | t-0101  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:11:00Z | 2026-11-23T09:12:40Z |
      When the counts are read at 2026-11-23T09:15:30Z
      Then zone 161 shows 2 trips requested between 09:10 and 09:15
```

#### Show one behaviour in each example

Test one behaviour in each example, as the behave documentation recommends
([behave: scenarios](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#scenarios)): when the example fails, its name
tells you which situation broke it. If an example checks two unrelated outcomes, split it into two examples, under the rules they
show.

#### Put a number or a fixed answer in the Then

The `Then` compares what the system produced with an answer that is known before the run. You chose the data, so
you know the answer: the table above holds two different `event_id` values, so 2 must be counted.

| Then that a test cannot check | Then with a number or a fixed answer |
|---|---|
| `Then the counts look right` | `Then zone 161 shows 2 trips requested between 09:10 and 09:15` |
| `Then the quiet zone is handled` | `Then zone 48 shows no data between 09:25 and 09:30` |
| `Then the late request is handled` | `Then zone 161 has 2 trips requested between 09:00 and 09:05` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[36,64]"}

### Testing LLM answers {#testing-model-answers}

An LLM's answer can differ between runs, so one example with a fixed reply does not show a requirement on it. An
**eval** runs the LLM's part of your system on a set of cases with known answers, each case several times, and
counts the runs with a correct answer. The rule gets one **gate example**: an example tagged `@eval` whose steps
name the eval of your `## Evals` section in `docs/requirements.md`, its number of cases, the runs of each case, and
how many runs must be correct; it fails when fewer runs are correct. Beside it go ordinary examples, each with one
input and the answer that the rule allows, such as a message that names only a destination.

```gherkin
@JS04 @assistant
Feature: Pickup place of a rider's message
  Covers JS04 (support agent) in a system that includes the assistant, our extension. The assistant sends the
  rider's message to the model as the user message; the output format is a JSON object with one field,
  pickup_place: a name from evals/pickup_place/places.txt, null when the message names no pickup place, or
  "more than one" when it names more than one.
  Step code: this example repository has step code for this feature only, to show how an LLM eval runs in behave.
  You do not write step code for Checkpoint 1.

  @R110
  Rule: Where the system includes the assistant, when a support agent opens a rider's message, the system shall show the pickup place that the message names, as a name from our list of places, or say that the message names no pickup place

    Example: Message that names a pickup place
      Given the rider message "I'm waiting outside JFK Terminal 4, door 6. Where is my driver?"
      When the support agent opens the message
      Then the pickup place is "JFK Terminal 4"

    Example: Message that names only a destination
      Given the rider message "Take me to Penn Station. I haven't decided where to be picked up yet."
      When the support agent opens the message
      Then the system says that the message names no pickup place

    @eval
    Example: Eval of pickup places
      Given the 10 cases of the eval "pickup-place"
      When the model that the system uses answers each case 3 times
      Then the pickup place is correct in at least 24 of the 30 runs

  @R120
  Rule: If a rider's message names more than one pickup place, then the system shall say that the message names more than one pickup place, and not show any of them as the pickup place

    Example: Message that names two pickup places
      Given the rider message "Pick me up at Penn Station or at Grand Central Terminal, whichever is faster for the driver."
      When the support agent opens the message
      Then the system says that the message names more than one pickup place
```

### Dry run and how to read its output {#dry-run}

A **dry run** makes behave read every feature file and look for the code of every step, without running a step
([behave: command-line arguments](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/behave/#command-line-arguments), `--dry-run`).
`uvx` runs behave without adding it to your project.

1. At the root of your repository, run:

   ```default
   uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run
   ```

2. Read the output from the top. If your file holds only the R020 rule and its example, you should see:

```default
USING RUNNER: behave.runner:Runner
@JS01
Feature: Trips requested in each zone # features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature:2
  Covers the first part of JS01 (operations analyst): the number of trips requested in each pickup zone for each
  5-minute period. A period holds the requests with an event time from its start up to, and not including, its end.
    Example: Request received 7 minutes late                      # features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature:9
      Given only these trip requests are received:                # None
        | event_id  | trip_id | pickup_zone_id | event_time           | received_time        |
        | ev-000011 | t-0011  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:01:10Z | 2026-11-23T09:01:11Z |
        | ev-000012 | t-0012  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:04:00Z | 2026-11-23T09:11:00Z |
      When the time is 2026-11-23T09:11:30Z                       # None
      Then zone 161 has 2 trips requested between 09:00 and 09:05 # None


You can implement step definitions for undefined steps with these snippets:

from behave.api.pending_step import StepNotImplementedError
@given(u'only these trip requests are received:')
def step_impl(context):
    raise StepNotImplementedError(u'Given only these trip requests are received:')


@when(u'the time is 2026-11-23T09:11:30Z')
def step_impl(context):
    raise StepNotImplementedError(u'When the time is 2026-11-23T09:11:30Z')


@then(u'zone 161 has 2 trips requested between 09:00 and 09:05')
def step_impl(context):
    raise StepNotImplementedError(u'Then zone 161 has 2 trips requested between 09:00 and 09:05')



Errored scenarios:
  features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature:9  Request received 7 minutes late

0 features passed, 0 failed, 1 error, 0 skipped
0 rules passed, 0 failed, 1 error, 0 skipped
0 scenarios passed, 0 failed, 1 error, 0 skipped
0 steps passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 3 undefined
Took 0min 0.000s
```

| Part of the output | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Feature, example and steps, each with a file name and a line number | behave read the file. Check that every example you wrote is listed. The dry run does not print the `Rule:` lines or their tags. |
| `# None` after a step | behave did not find code for this step. At Level 0 every step has `# None`. |
| Snippets under `You can implement step definitions` | A code snippet for each step without code. You write these functions at Level 1. |
| `Errored scenarios` and `1 error` | An example with a step without code is marked as errored. |
| `1 error` in the `rules` line | A rule with an errored example is counted as errored. |
| `3 undefined` | The number of steps without code: the three steps of the example. A table belongs to the step above it. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

For a draft, this is the result you want: every example is listed and errored, and every step is undefined,
because the steps do not have code yet. The command's exit code is 1 for the same reason. Check that the `rules`
count matches your `Rule:` lines. The `scenarios` count includes each `Example:` or `Scenario:` line and each data
row of a `Scenario Outline:`. To count the lines, run `grep -hE "^ *(Example|Scenario):" features/*.feature | wc -l`.

To see the list without the snippets, add `--no-snippets`:

```default
uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run --no-snippets
```

For the rides example, four feature files with 22 examples, the last lines are:

```default
0 features passed, 0 failed, 3 error, 0 skipped, 1 untested
0 rules passed, 0 failed, 12 error, 0 skipped, 2 untested
0 scenarios passed, 0 failed, 18 error, 0 skipped, 4 untested
0 steps passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 73 undefined, 11 untested
Took 0min 0.000s
```

The JS04 feature, its 2 rules and its 4 examples are `untested`: the example repository has step code for that
feature (`features/steps/pickup_steps.py`), and a dry run does not run it. The last step of R120's example does not
have code yet, so it is one of the 73 `undefined`. Your team does not write step code for Checkpoint 1, so you see
every example as `error`.

These results mean that the draft needs a fix:

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `ConfigError: No steps directory in '.../features'` | The folder `features/steps/` is missing. | Create it as in [Folder layout](#folder-layout). |
| `ParserError: Failed to parse ".../features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature":` and `Parser failure in state=steps at line 14: "Whn the time is 2026-11-23T09:11:30Z"` | A line is not Gherkin. behave stops before it lists an example. | Fix the line that the message names. Here `When` is misspelled. |
| An example lists fewer steps than you wrote, and the `undefined` count is lower than your number of steps | The first step of that example has a misspelled keyword, such as `Givn`. behave reads the line as free text and does not report an error. | Compare the steps listed under each example with your file. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[40,30,30]"}

### Feature files of the rides example {#whole-example}

The rides example has four job stories and the four feature files of the [folder layout](#folder-layout) above, with
14 rules and 22 examples. JS01 is served by two feature files. "One driver for each trip" serves JS02 and JS03, so
its rules are written once, and its rule for R080 carries the constraint RF030 as a second tag. Part of its
`docs/requirements.md` and of its `features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature` is on the
[Checkpoint 1](project-checkpoint1.qmd#requirements) page.

Here is part of
[`features/trip_assignment.feature`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/cp1-example/blob/cp1/features/trip_assignment.feature?plain=1#L1-L32):
a rule with two IDs, and an example in which two drivers accept the same trip and both accepts are sent before
either driver has an answer:

```gherkin
@JS02 @JS03
Feature: One driver for each trip
  Covers JS02 (driver): whether the trip I accepted is mine.
  Covers JS03 (rider): which driver is coming.
  A table holds the only events of its example. Its columns are event fields listed in docs/design.md, section Data.
  An accept is one request to our API. A simulated data set is named by its id and described in the same section.

  # (rule R070 is left out here)

  @R080 @RF030
  Rule: If a driver accepts a trip that is already assigned, then the system shall refuse the accept and leave the trip with its driver

    Example: Two drivers accept at the same time
      Given only these trip requests are received:
        | event_id  | trip_id | pickup_zone_id | event_time           | received_time        |
        | ev-000310 | t-0303  | 161            | 2026-11-23T09:20:00Z | 2026-11-23T09:20:01Z |
      When these accepts are sent together, each before the other has an answer:
        | event_id  | trip_id | driver_id | event_time           | received_time        |
        | ev-000311 | t-0303  | d-0046    | 2026-11-23T09:20:05Z | 2026-11-23T09:20:06Z |
        | ev-000312 | t-0303  | d-0131    | 2026-11-23T09:20:04Z | 2026-11-23T09:20:06Z |
      Then trip t-0303 is assigned to exactly one of drivers d-0046 and d-0131
      And 1 accept is refused
```

All four feature files are in the `features/` folder of [cp1-example](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/cp1-example/tree/cp1/features)
(tag `cp1`).

## Level 1 (Checkpoint 2, proposed): a first step function {#level-1}

::: {.callout-tip title="Practise it in tutorial B5T2"}
[Tutorial B5T2](tutorials.qmd#b5-t2) ([repository](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b5-t2-behave-sim)) walks
through this level on the rides example: you write three step functions by hand, have your coding assistant write
the steps of a second rule and check them, then run a scenario on a simulated data set whose expected value comes from
its truth. After the section, B5 makes a simulated data set for your own project.
:::

At this level you write the Python code that makes each step do something. A **step function** is a Python
function that behave calls when it reaches a step with a matching text. Build the example below once in an empty
folder outside your repository, then do the same for your own scenarios.

The example tests one small function, `count_requests`, with a scenario of four steps. To stay short, it puts the
tag `@RF010` on a `Scenario:` without a `Rule:`; in your repository, your examples stay under the rules of their
IDs. The example has these files:

```default
behave-first-step/
├── rides.py                     the code under test
└── features/
    ├── request_counts.feature   the scenario
    ├── environment.py           setup and teardown
    └── steps/
        └── request_steps.py     the step functions
```

### Code under test and its scenario

1. In a terminal, move to the folder that holds your repository's folder (`cd ..` from the root of your
   repository). Create the example folder there and move into it:

   ```default
   mkdir -p behave-first-step/features/steps
   cd behave-first-step
   pwd
   ```

   You should see a path that ends in `/behave-first-step`. Run every command of this level in this folder.

2. Create `rides.py` with the code below. The function reads a file with one trip request on each line and counts
   the requests of each pickup zone. A request that arrives twice has the same `event_id` both times, and the
   function skips an `event_id` it has already seen. After you save the file, run `ls rides.py`. You should see
   `rides.py` listed.

   ```python
   import json


   def count_requests(path):
       seen = set()
       counts = {}
       for line in open(path):
           request = json.loads(line)
           if request["event_id"] in seen:
               continue
           seen.add(request["event_id"])
           zone = request["pickup_zone_id"]
           counts[zone] = counts.get(zone, 0) + 1
       return counts
   ```

3. Create `features/request_counts.feature` with the scenario below. After you save it, run
   `ls features/request_counts.feature`. You should see the file listed.

   ```gherkin
   @JS01
   Feature: Trips requested in each zone
     When demand moves between zones, I want the number of trips requested in each
     pickup zone, so that I can send free drivers where the requests are.

     @RF010
     Scenario: A request that arrives twice
       Given riders in zone 161 request 6 trips
       And the simulator delivers 2 of the requests a second time
       When the requests are counted
       Then zone 161 has 6 trips requested
   ```

   A step that starts with `And` continues the kind of step above it
   ([behave: And, But](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/gherkin/#and-but)). Here the `And` line is a second `Given`.

4. Run `uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run --no-snippets`. You should see the four steps with `# None`, and the last lines:

   ```default
   0 features passed, 0 failed, 1 error, 0 skipped
   0 scenarios passed, 0 failed, 1 error, 0 skipped
   0 steps passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 4 undefined
   Took 0min 0.000s
   ```

### Setup and teardown in environment.py

Some work belongs to every scenario and to none of its steps: creating an empty folder or table before the
scenario, and removing it after. behave reads a file `features/environment.py` and calls the functions in it
that have fixed names, called **hooks**: `before_scenario` runs before each scenario and `after_scenario` runs
after it. There are also `before_all`, `after_all`, `before_feature` and `after_feature`
([behave: environmental controls](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/#environmental-controls)).

Every hook and every step function receives `context` as its first argument. **`context`** is an object on which
you store what a later step needs, as attributes: `context.requests_file = ...`. behave empties it of the values
of a scenario when the scenario ends, so one scenario does not see the data of another
([behave: context](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/#context)).

5. Create `features/environment.py` with the two hooks below. After you save it, run `ls features/environment.py`.
   You should see the file listed.

   ```python
   import tempfile
   from pathlib import Path


   def before_scenario(context, scenario):
       # Setup: every scenario gets an empty folder of its own for the requests file.
       context.folder = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
       context.requests_file = Path(context.folder.name) / "requests.jsonl"


   def after_scenario(context, scenario):
       # Teardown: runs after the scenario, also when a step failed.
       context.folder.cleanup()
   ```

### Step functions with parameters

A step function has a decorator, `@given`, `@when` or `@then`, with the text of the step. A part of the text in
curly brackets is a **parameter**: behave takes the value from the scenario's line and passes it to the function
as an argument. `{name}` gives text, and `{n:d}` gives a whole number
([behave: step parameters](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/#step-parameters)). One function then
serves every scenario that uses the same sentence with other values.

6. Create `features/steps/request_steps.py` with the code below. The file name is your choice: behave loads every
   `.py` file in `features/steps/`
   ([behave: Python step implementations](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/#python-step-implementations)).
   After you save it, run `ls features/steps/request_steps.py`. You should see the file listed.

   ```python
   import json

   from behave import given, then, when

   from rides import count_requests


   @given("riders in zone {zone:d} request {n:d} trips")
   def step_riders_request(context, zone, n):
       context.requests = [
           {"event_id": f"ev-{i:06d}", "pickup_zone_id": zone} for i in range(n)
       ]
       _write(context)


   @given("the simulator delivers {n:d} of the requests a second time")
   def step_delivered_twice(context, n):
       context.requests += context.requests[:n]
       _write(context)


   @when("the requests are counted")
   def step_count(context):
       context.counts = count_requests(context.requests_file)


   @then("zone {zone:d} has {n:d} trips requested")
   def step_check_count(context, zone, n):
       actual = context.counts[zone]
       assert actual == n, f"zone {zone}: expected {n}, actual {actual}"


   def _write(context):
       lines = [json.dumps(request) for request in context.requests]
       context.requests_file.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
   ```

   Read the four functions against the four steps of the scenario:

   | Step in the scenario | Function | What it does |
   |---|---|---|
   | `Given riders in zone 161 request 6 trips` | `step_riders_request(context, 161, 6)` | Writes 6 requests into the file that the setup named. |
   | `And the simulator delivers 2 of the requests a second time` | `step_delivered_twice(context, 2)` | Adds the first 2 requests to the file again: the injected fault. |
   | `When the requests are counted` | `step_count(context)` | Calls the code under test and keeps its result in `context.counts`. |
   | `Then zone 161 has 6 trips requested` | `step_check_count(context, 161, 6)` | Compares the result with the number in the step. A failed `assert` fails the step. |

   : {tbl-colwidths="[36,32,32]"}

### Run the scenario

7. Run behave without `--dry-run`:

   ```default
   uvx behave@1.3.3
   ```

   You should see each step followed by the file and the line of its function, and all four steps passed:

   ```default
     @RF010
     Scenario: A request that arrives twice                       # features/request_counts.feature:7
       Given riders in zone 161 request 6 trips                   # features/steps/request_steps.py:8
       And the simulator delivers 2 of the requests a second time # features/steps/request_steps.py:16
       When the requests are counted                              # features/steps/request_steps.py:22
       Then zone 161 has 6 trips requested                        # features/steps/request_steps.py:27

   1 feature passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped
   1 scenario passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped
   4 steps passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped
   Took 0min 0.001s
   ```

8. Check that the scenario can fail. In `rides.py`, replace the line `if request["event_id"] in seen:` with
   `if False:`, so that the function counts every line, and run `uvx behave@1.3.3` again. You should see the `Then` step
   fail with both numbers:

   ```default
       Then zone 161 has 6 trips requested                        # features/steps/request_steps.py:27
         ASSERT FAILED: zone 161: expected 6, actual 8



   Failing scenarios:
     features/request_counts.feature:7  A request that arrives twice

   0 features passed, 1 failed, 0 skipped
   0 scenarios passed, 1 failed, 0 skipped
   3 steps passed, 1 failed, 0 skipped
   Took 0min 0.001s
   ```

   The message names the zone, the expected number and the actual number, because the `assert` in the `Then`
   function has a message. Write one for every `assert`.

9. Put the line `if request["event_id"] in seen:` back and run `uvx behave@1.3.3` once more. You should see
   `1 scenario passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped`.

### From the example to your repository

In your repository, the snippets that the dry run prints are the starting point:

1. Copy the snippets into a Python file in `features/steps/`.
2. Add `from behave import given, when, then` at the top of the file.
3. Replace each `raise` line with code. Where two steps differ only in a value, write one function with a
   parameter.
4. Run `uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run --no-snippets`. You should see the file and the line of a function after each step
   that has code, in place of `# None`.

To run the scenarios of one ID, name its tag: `uvx behave@1.3.3 --tags=RF010`
([behave: tag expressions](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tag_expressions/)).

If your step code imports packages that your project installs with uv, run behave inside the project with
`uv add --dev behave` once and then `uv run behave`.

### Step functions in l19-events

In [`l19-events`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events), open
[`features/steps/steps.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/features/steps/steps.py) and
[`features/environment.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/features/environment.py). The
`Given` functions read the files that the simulator wrote, the `When` functions call the code under test, and the
`Then` functions compare the result with the simulator's known answer.

## Level 2 (later, proposed): steps from the course kit {#level-2}

A course kit with ready steps for the simulator, DuckDB queries and evals comes with Checkpoint 2. With the kit,
many of your scenarios do not need step code of your own: you write a step in the kit's wording, and the kit's
function runs it.

What you do at this level:

1. After you have set up the kit that comes with Checkpoint 2 in your repository, list the steps that already have
   code, before you write a new step function. At the root of your repository, run:

   ```default
   uvx behave@1.3.3 --steps-catalog
   ```

   You should see one line for each step text, with its parameters in curly brackets
   ([behave: command-line arguments](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/behave/#command-line-arguments),
   `--steps-catalog`). In the Level 1 example folder, the same command lists:

   ```default
   Given riders in zone {zone:d} request {n:d} trips

   Given the simulator delivers {n:d} of the requests a second time

   When the requests are counted

   Then zone {zone:d} has {n:d} trips requested
   ```

2. Where a listed step says what your scenario needs, change your scenario's line to that wording. Run
   `uvx behave@1.3.3 --dry-run --no-snippets`. You should see the file and the line of the step's function after that
   line, in place of `# None`.
3. For a step that the list does not cover, write a step function as at Level 1, and run the dry run again. You
   should see the new step with the line of your function.

### Simulator faults in l19-events

In [`l19-events`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events), open
[`events/README.md`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/events/README.md): it lists the
injected faults that the simulator writes and the file with the known answers that the `Then` steps compare with.

## Level 3 (later, proposed): live cloud runs and an eval as a gate {#level-3}

### Live cloud runs behind a tag

The scenarios of Levels 0 to 2 run on your laptop on simulated data. A scenario that calls your deployed system on
AWS is slower and spends money, so it runs only when you ask for it. The tag `@live` marks such a scenario, and
a settings file leaves the tag out of a normal run.

1. Put the live scenarios in a feature file of their own, with `@live` beside the story's tag, as shown below.
   After you save it, check its first line. You should see both `@JS01` and `@live`.

   ```gherkin
   @JS01 @live
   Feature: Trips requested in each zone, on AWS

     @RF010
     Scenario: A request that arrives twice at the deployed pipeline
       Given the counting pipeline is deployed in my AWS account
       When 6 trip requests for zone 161 are written to the stream and 2 of them a second time
       Then the counts table has 6 trips requested for zone 161
   ```

2. Create a file `behave.ini` at the root of your repository with the two lines below
   ([behave: configuration files](https://behave.readthedocs.io/en/latest/behave/#configuration-files)). After you
   save it, run `cat behave.ini`. You should see the line `default_tags = not @live`.

   ```default
   [behave]
   default_tags = not @live
   ```

3. Run `uvx behave@1.3.3`. You should see the live scenario skipped. With this feature beside the Level 1 example, the
   last lines are:

   ```default
   1 feature passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped
   1 scenario passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped
   4 steps passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped
   Took 0min 0.001s
   ```

4. When your system is deployed and the live steps have code, run only the live scenarios, at the root of your
   repository:

   ```default
   uvx behave@1.3.3 --tags=live
   ```

   You should see the steps of the `@live` scenarios run, and the other scenarios counted as skipped in the last
   lines.

A live scenario creates data in your account. Remove it in `after_scenario`, as the teardown at Level 1 does.

In your repository, an ID keeps one rule: a live example can sit under the rule of its ID instead, with `@live`
on the rule, as the rule of RF040 in `features/js01_trips_per_zone.feature` of the rides example.

### Eval as a gate

A part of your system that calls an LLM can give a different answer on each run, so a `Then` with one
fixed answer does not test it. An eval runs that part on a set of cases with known answers, each case several times.
A **gate** is a check that fails when fewer runs are correct than the number you chose. The gate is the `@eval`
example under the requirement's rule, as at [Level 0](#level-0): at this level its steps run the eval, or read a
saved eval run, and compare the number of correct runs with the number in its `Then`.

### Live runs and gates in l19-events and recipes

- Live runs: in [`l19-events`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events), open
  [`behave.ini`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/behave.ini) and
  [`features/js01_live.feature`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/features/js01_live.feature).
- Eval as a gate: in the public [recipes](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/recipes), open
  [`agent-agentcore/features/eval.feature`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/recipes/blob/main/agent-agentcore/features/eval.feature).
  In `l19-events`, open
  [`features/js02_eval.feature`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/l19-events/blob/main/features/js02_eval.feature).
